articles.title: EU leaders urged to 'act now' to stay AI competitive with US, China
articles.summary: EU leaders in Dublin were called on by an AI executive to move quickly in the tech race with the US and China. EU official Metsola, however, expressed frustration with the idea that the bloc is…

image.caption: EU leaders met in Dublin amid concerns that the bloc could be falling behind in AI development Image: Cathal McNaughton/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Union leaders met in Dublin on Friday at the first ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI). The meeting came at a critical moment, as the bloc seeks a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology.
The meeting took place in Dublin's Convention Center, which was also the meeting place of the European Political Community summit this week.
Mistral's CEO Mensch urges EU to 'act now'
French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch, as well as Nobel-prize winner and researcher Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," spoke to EU leaders at the summit.
"Europe has all the technology and the talent to lead the AI race," Mensch said during the event. "What it needs is speed, financing and a strong coordination between member states."
Mensch urged the leaders to "act now" to stay competitive with the US and China in regards to AI development.

"AI is the most important technology of our time," European Council ‌President Antonio Costa said in a post on X regarding the summit. "Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services. We must also manage the risks and changes it will bring — and help set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI."
The summit took place at a time of mounting worries about the emerging technology, which promises to transform ‌industries, labor markets and societies.
It also came in the wake of a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months and the wider discussion about how the technology could harm humanity.

Tech leaders behind the technology have also fallen under scrutiny. As recently as this week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign after it was revealed that he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company.
Finding Europe's role in the AI revolution
During the summit, a discussion occurred about where Europe fits in within the AI movement.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she frustrated with the notion that Europe had "somehow lost the AI race."
She noted that the EU has "world-class talent, technological expertise and industrial experience to lead in AI."
"What we need now is to ensure that our ideas have the financing they need to grow and succeed in Europe," she added.
Will AI laws protect us? EU AI Act explained
EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said there is a "dark side" to AI.

"We can all already see this in the battlefield in Ukraine, where you have drones equipped by artificial intelligence to really train to find anybody to kill," Kallas, the former prime minister of Estonia, said at the event.

Leaders face questions on how to unlock AI's potential, how to catch up with China and the United States in the race for the technology, but also how to protect against the risks it poses to individuals and businesses.

The governments of Estonia and Finland wrote in a letter ahead of the summit that Europe must "establish EU-level arrangements for responding to serious AI incidents," calling for "developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly."

articles.title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
articles.summary:
Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems

The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one…

blocks.text: The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

blocks.caption: Albert Einstein presenting Kurt Gödel (second from right) with an award at Princeton University, where the two became friends. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann Archive

blocks.text: “I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”

Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.

In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.

In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.

“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.
“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A microfilm image of an example of Gödel’s  shorthand from one of his notebooks. Photograph: Institute for Advanced Study

blocks.text: Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.
Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.

The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.

“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”

Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice he would have won the 1940 Fields medal.
“Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”

In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About fifty were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! or schlecht! [bad].”

Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”

Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”

He said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

articles.title: Chuck Schumer’s challenger for party control underscores Democrats’ ideological rift
articles.summary: Senator Chris Van Hollen’s policy credentials allowed his quick rise to roles usually reserved for the more tenured

blocks.text: US senator Chris Van Hollen’s challenge to Chuck Schumer’s leadership of Senate Democrats presents an ideological and biographical contrast to the party as it takes control of Congress in two months.

Though only about eight years younger than Schumer, Van Hollen is seen as a more progressive senator who has drawn attention for his opposition to the Trump administration’s abusive immigration practices – visiting his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García after an unlawful deportation to El Salvador – as well as opposition to federal corruption and US support for the Israeli government’s war in Gaza.

Van Hollen’s father was a diplomat and his mother was a spy. Born in Karachi and raised abroad before returning to the US for high school in Massachusetts, Van Hollen, 67, earned a philosophy degree from Swarthmore College, then a masters of public policy concentrating in national security studies from Harvard’s John F Kennedy school of government. He worked as a US Senate staffer while studying for a law degree from Georgetown University, which he earned in 1990.

He won a seat in the Maryland house of delegates in the same year, representing Montgomery county, and developed a reputation for fierce advocacy for environmental causes, gun control and public education. Four years later, he won a state senate seat, which he held until challenging a popular moderate Republican congresswoman, Constance A Morella, in 2002. Democrats nationally took a beating that year; Van Hollen’s success was an outlier.

Van Hollen’s policy credentials and longstanding political relationships allowed him to rise quickly into congressional leadership roles usually reserved for more tenured congresspeople. He chaired the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the House fundraising arm for electing Democrats, taking over for Rahm Emanuel in 2008. Van Hollen was a key congressional negotiator during the Great Financial Crisis.

When US senator Barbara Mikulski retired after 30 years in office in 2016, Van Hollen emerged as the favored successor by Maryland’s political establishment and had the support of Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid. Van Hollen became the Senate’s chief fundraiser.

Despite this role, Van Hollen has long opposed the Citizens United ruling that opened the floodgates for corporate spending on political campaigns. Van Hollen was one of dozens of lawmakers who filed an amicus brief in the case to defend federal spending limits and has repeatedly called for a constitutional amendment to overturn the decision.

Van Hollen has also been one of senate Democrats’ sharpest critics of the Israeli government and its actions in Gaza. Long a supporter of a two-state solution, Van Hollen visited the Rafah crossing between Egypt and Gaza in January 2024 to observe aid shipments, declaring the assistance process “broken”. Van Hollen subsequently voted for a resolution proposed by US senator Bernie Sanders to apply the human rights provisions of the Foreign Assistance Act to US military aid to Israel. The resolution failed 72-11, with most Democrats also opposing the measure.

Van Hollen authored a report in November 2025 which described the war as a “plan to ethnically cleanse Gaza of Palestinians”, and that “America is complicit.” Van Hollen has worked to end arms shipments to Israel and opposes American security agreements with Israel in the National Defense Authorization Act.
Van Hollen is also a critic of cryptocurrency and decentralized finance in ways that distinguish him from Schumer and Democratic political ties to the New York financial markets.

“As we’ve seen time and again, cryptocurrency and digital assets are rife with opportunity for abuse if left unchecked,” Van Hollen said in a statement opposing the Clarity Act, a financial regulatory package offered by Republicans. Van Hollen has pursued legislation to ban federal officials from owning or promoting cryptocurrency, pointedly highlighting the president’s billion-dollar gains.

Speaking in post-election interviews last week, Van Hollen argued that Democrats “should not be overly cautious in going after corporations, billionaires and special interests that voters blame for making their lives harder”.

articles.title: What's going on with the polar vortex?
articles.summary: Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it…

image.caption: Cold snaps during winter can sometimes be linked to disruptions to the polar vortexImage: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.
If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.
Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.
Earliest vortex disruption on record
It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.
The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

blocks.caption: When the polar vortex is detabilized, it can send a blast of freezing temperatures further southImage: Adam Glanzman/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: What exactly is the polar vortex and how does it work?
The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.
So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.
This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.
It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.
What does this mean for winter weather?

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.
Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.
For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.
What happens when El Nino meets climate change?

articles.title: Jaguar Land Rover reports £451m quarterly loss after cutting 4,000 jobs
articles.summary:
JLR chief executive calls for EU and Britain to join forces amid competition from Chinese electric carmakers

Jaguar Land Rover has reported a £451m quarterly loss as it counts the cost of…

blocks.text: Jaguar Land Rover has reported a £451m quarterly loss as it counts the cost of cutting 4,000 jobs, while its chief executive has called for the EU and Britain to work together in the face of competition from China.

Britain’s largest automotive employer reported revenues rising to £5.9bn between July and September, but it recorded £530m in costs from the job cuts announced near the end of that period amid tough trading conditions.
JLR said it expected the vast majority of the job cuts to be achieved via voluntary redundancies, with 3,000 already confirmed. Most of those people will leave at the end of November.
JLR said it had scraped into profit from its operations if it ignored the restructuring costs, but it was hurt by falling sales in China and the Middle East.
Many European carmakers are struggling as they face competition from Chinese rivals at the same time as they invest in electric car production.

blocks.caption: JLR’s electric Range Rover is one of its first electric models.  Photograph: JLR Media

blocks.text: PB Balaji, JLR’s chief executive, said on Friday the “onslaught of competition” from China meant the UK and EU should stop plans for new post-Brexit trade barriers on each other.

The automotive industry is lobbying the UK and EU intensely to delay the implementation of “rules of origin” on 1 January, which threaten to impose 10% tariffs on UK-EU electric cars that use batteries from Asia. The EU is also considering “made in Europe” rules that would lock UK-made cars out of subsidies.

“Now is the time for actually fostering this entire electrical ecosystem,” Balaji said. “It’s so important for us that we all hold hands, stick together and ensure that we get the system to evolve into the world of electrics.”
He added: “We just need time to ensure all these plans start coming into fruition.”

The company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata, previously sought to target China for growth, only to write off billions in investments in 2019 as a new wave of Chinese carmakers led to massive overcapacity in the country.
after newsletter promotion

JLR, which was last year hit by a devastating hack, is targeting growth in the US, where it is in the process of agreeing a deal for the Chrysler owner, Stellantis, to manufacture Land Rovers for the first time.

JLR has started to produce electric Land Rovers, beginning with its flagship Range Rover, built in Solihull in the West Midlands. Electric versions of its cheaper, higher-selling Range Rover Sport, Defender and Defender Sport will follow.
It also produces the luxury electric Jaguar Type 01, and Balaji said JLR was working on a new version of the Discovery.

articles.title: Richard Neil found guilty in 1990s 'woodland rapist' cold case
articles.summary: A three-decade search for a predator dubbed southern Ontario's "woodland rapist" has ended with a Toronto man convicted of kidnapping and sexual assault.

image.caption: A composite sketch, left, released by police in 1995 illustrated the description of an unknown attacker who had targeted three children in southern Ontario parks between 1992 and 1995. Richard Neil, right, is seen in a picture released by police following his arrest in Toronto in 2024. (Halton Regio

blocks.text: Toronto·Breaking
A three-decade search for a predator dubbed southern Ontario's "woodland rapist" has ended with a Toronto man convicted of kidnapping and sexual assault.
Toronto man, 67, convicted of 17 offences in connection with attacks that long baffled police
WARNING: This story contains details of sexual assault against children.

A jury at the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton on Friday found Richard Neil guilty of a total of 17 offences in connection with three brutal attacks on children in public parks in 1992, 1994 and 1995.

Two boys, aged 8 and 10, and a 15-year-old girl each told police they'd been lured into wooded areas, tied up and raped by a stranger. The victims all said they'd been forced to drink the assailant's urine.

Once DNA evidence showed the same unknown suspect had carried out all three attacks in the Ontario communities of Kitchener, Brampton and Oakville, police launched an urgent search to identify the man and catch him.
Nearly 30 years went by without a significant break in the case — until advances in forensic technology led to Neil's arrest in 2024.
Richard Neil leaves a Brampton, Ont., courthouse on Oct. 16. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
At the time, police announced there may be more victims.
The 67-year-old Neil, a British-born former Canada Post and UPS driver, had homes in Toronto and Victoria, B.C.
The divorced father of three insisted he wasn't involved in the 1990s assaults. But the evidence — including DNA, fingerprints and Neil's interest in urine-drinking — was hard to dispute.
It took the jury less than four hours of deliberation to unanimously accept the Crown's version of events.
Neil will be sentenced at a later date.
"There's some relief of course, mixed with a little bit of disappointment that we couldn't catch him at the time," retired Halton Regional Police Det. Sgt. Graham Barnes told CBC News.
A Halton Regional police officer is seen in 1995 holding a composite sketch of the then-unknown child sex predator dubbed the 'woodland rapist.' (CBC)
Longtime cold case

The case long baffled investigators from the Peel, Halton and Waterloo regions, who formed the Project Woodland task force in 1995. As the manhunt made headlines at the time, the media labelled the unidentified attacker the "woodland rapist," given his pattern of violence.
A composite sketch of a man — based on descriptions provided by the victims — was distributed to law enforcement agencies across the province and nearby U.S. states.

Officers canvassed Oakville neighbourhoods nightly in 1995 and reportedly received more than 1,300 tips over the years. Neil's trial heard that the Centre of Forensic Sciences in Toronto had looked at 310 persons of interest in total — to no avail.
At one point, Barnes, the former lead detective said he even hired a Texas-based firm to see if a Russian satellite had captured an image of a licence plate on an SUV linked to the attacker.
DNA on underwear worn as mask helped identify alleged child rapist
By 1999, police speculated the assailant could be dead.
But Crown attorney Shazin Karim told the jury police finally identified Neil as a suspect in recent years thanks to genetic genealogy analysis conducted in the U.S.
The investigative technique — which involves comparing crime scene DNA to genetic data voluntarily submitted to direct-to-consumer genealogical services — was unavailable to police in the 1990s.
One of the victims previously told CBC News that according to investigators, the breakthrough was made possible after one of Neil's relatives submitted their DNA to an ancestry-type website.
The victim, who was 10 when he was assaulted in Brampton's Norton Place Park in 1994, said he was "shaking" when he was told of Neil's arrest.
"I felt overwhelmed with joy, then sadness," he said, "as I started to recall the memories of that day."

In September 1994, Peel Regional Police said a boy was walking through Brampton's Norton Place Park when he was approached by a suspect and lured to a nearby wooded area, where he was sexually assaulted. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Neil's trial before Justice Rosemarie Juginovic began in early October. The jury heard contemporaneous police interviews of the three victims, who were not required to testify. Their identities are covered by a court-ordered publication ban.
Three horrific attacks
The unsolved attacks on children sent shockwaves through southern Ontario communities in the 1990s.

On Aug. 21, 1992, an eight-year-old boy told police he'd been approached by a man offering to show him a collection of bikes in a wooded area of Kitchener's Idlewood Park. The man later pulled out a pocket knife and tied the boy's foot to a tree before sexually assaulting him.
On Sept. 29, 1994, the 10-year-old boy reported a similar attack in the Brampton park. He said he was forced to drink urine from a bottle and perform sex acts on the man.

The jury in the trial of Richard Neil was shown this image of a two-litre pop bottle recovered from the scene of a brutal attack on a 15-year-old girl at Wildwood Park in Oakville, Ont., on Aug. 31, 1995. The girl told police the unknown assailant forced her to drink urine from the bottle. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)

Then, on Aug. 31, 1995, a 15-year-old girl recounted another violent incident with further similarities, including the use of a bottle for urine-drinking. The court heard she was held at gunpoint and also made to snort cocaine.
Prosecutors said forensic analysis showed it's "20 quadrillion times more likely" that DNA collected at the three crime scenes belonged to Neil, rather than another, random person.
The jury was told Neil's fingerprints matched those lifted from two shopping bags and a two-litre pop bottle located at Wildwood Park in Oakville, where the girl was assaulted.
What's more, Karim, the Crown attorney, said images, videos and messages seized from Neil's electronic devices demonstrated he has "an interest in urine-drinking."
Neil acknowledged having a "simple fetish" for urine, insisting "it's actually quite common." He said he had only "engaged in that act" with consenting adults.
With files from Dana Roberts

articles.title: Met police launch investigation into David Walliams allegations
articles.summary:
Police say allegations of sexual misconduct are separate from those made by multiple women in Guardian and ITN investigation

The Metropolitan police have announced a criminal investigation…
articles.byline: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

blocks.text: The Metropolitan police have announced a criminal investigation into David Walliams over alleged sexual misconduct.
In reports by the Guardian and ITV News, Walliams, 55, has been accused by multiple women of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex.
Details of the allegations were revealed after a court rejected a legal attempt by Walliams aimed at preventing publication. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Walliams is one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors.

In a statement announcing the criminal investigation, the Met said the serious allegations it was investigating were separate from those reported by news organisations. “In recent days, the Met has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s.
“Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers.

“The allegations are separate from those reported by ITN and the Guardian. However, as part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences.”

Det Supt Mike Cagney, whose team is leading the investigation, said: “We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.
“We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process.”
People could report information to police by calling 101 and providing the reference 4900/10NOV26, or by contacting the complex sexual offences unit on 0207 175 2738.
More details soon …

articles.title: Ice hockey: Russia threatens against Canada and Germany over exclusion from tournaments
articles.summary: A fortnight after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two…

image.caption: While the Russia-based KHL remains one of the world's top leagues, Russia has been excluded from international play for yearsImage: Peter Kovalev/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.
"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak added after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.
"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

blocks.caption: Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak was the Soviet Union's top netminder in the 1970s and early 1980sImage: Yuri Kochetkov/SNA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Canada refuses to bend on junior tournament
The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed on Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to play in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Canadian Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said in a statement. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following last month's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling, in which it said that the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient – the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

Norway then said it had been bumped from the World Juniors and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated that they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.
Men's tournament with Russia 'effectively impossible'

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14. With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."
However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport said on Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the (German) ice hockey federation (DEB), nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a World Championship anywhere."
At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport—and ice hockey in particular—find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."
Munich's Olympic bid and the IOC's new stance on Russia

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hardline on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to pointing the way forward for the men's tournament in Germany next May.

articles.title: UK-EU deal will ‘dissolve’ £60m a year of costs for plant trade, says Angela Eagle
articles.summary:
Signing of agreement to smooth movement of food, plants and animals next week will not recoup huge sums firms were forced to spend

The removal of border checks and paperwork on plant imports…

blocks.text: The removal of border checks and paperwork on plant imports will “dissolve” £60m of annual costs for the horticulture industry when the UK and EU’s new post-Brexit deal comes in, the environment secretary has said.

Before the UK-EU summit on 20 November, Angela Eagle said she hopes paperwork headaches for importers will “disappear” after the changes, although the move will not help businesses recoup the large sums they spent to deal with border controls.

“If we get the ink dry on 20 November, which I very much hope we will … all of that uncertainty, the extra cost, the paperwork and the potential problems if things get stuck at borders would all disappear,” Eagle told the Guardian during a visit to a plant nursery in Kent.
“The cost, that £60m, can just dissolve and people’s potential to both export back into the EU and get their imports in … gets easier and more predictable.”
The UK’s departure from the bloc triggered the introduction of border checks on imports and exports of plants, food and animal products, from sausages and cheese to trees and leather goods.

Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit, according to analysis by the National Farmers’ Union, with egg, chicken and potato producers badly affected.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal, largely agreed between the two sides in May, is due to be signed at next week’s summit. It will permit the removal of the vast majority of physical checks and most of the accompanying certificates and paperwork.

This will save businesses in the horticulture sector the current cost of trading with Europe, including plant health inspection fees, phytosanitary certificates, document and ID checks, port fees, agents’ fees, additional labour costs and extra haulage costs.

These costs total £60m a year, according to calculations by the industry body the Horticultural Trades Association (HTA), but do not include late delivery penalties or sales lost because of port delays or damage to goods.
These savings should put “downward pressure on food prices”, Eagle said, although she would not confirm the deal would lower the cost of food in the UK.

The promise of the deal was welcomed by Provender Nurseries, one of the UK’s largest wholesale nurseries, which sells thousands of plants, trees and shrubs to local authorities, parks and landscapers from its base at Swanley in Kent.
However, the company has already spent at least £500,000 on building a post-Brexit control post on its eight-hectare (20-acre) site, which will become obsolete once the deal is implemented.

blocks.caption: Richard McKenna, the managing director of Provender, hopes the UK-EU deal will convince some of its European suppliers to restart exports. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: Richard McKenna, the managing director of Provender, said the business constructed the “sealed building and bought four electric forklifts to operate in it” to allow inspections of lorry loads of valuable trees and shrubs imported from the continent.
The company decided to build the site to reduce the “delays and damage” it has experienced when smaller loads are inspected at government-run border control posts such as Sevington.
“It cost a lot for a barn, but it gave us security as a business,” said McKenna.

Despite this, McKenna hopes the SPS deal will convince some of Provender’s European suppliers, previously deterred by the paperwork and potential pitfalls of post-Brexit trade with the UK, to restart exports.
“We need to see the small print on the agreement,” he said. “It could have been sooner, but we are pleased that it is happening.”
The deal is not expected to be implemented until the first quarter of 2028, meaning businesses such as Provender will still be subject to the current border arrangements for more than a year.
after newsletter promotion

In the meantime, Fran Barnes, the chief executive of the HTA, called for “some easements as a transition arrangement that are pragmatic” to help horticulture businesses, such as fewer or no checks on imports of lower-risk products.
Eagle conceded the implementation date was later than the mid-2027 targeted when former prime minister Keir Starmer announced his EU “reset” deal in May 2025.
Starmer’s replacement by Andy Burnham led to a “pause” in negotiations with Brussels, said Eagle, with the upcoming November summit pushed back from July.

The original target was “always a very, very ambitious timescale,” she said. “That extra time has meant we could deal in more coherent way with some of the knottier, thornier issues on things like pesticides.”
The UK has continued to use some pesticides and fungicides that are banned in the EU.

This has prompted industry concerns that British potatoes grown in 2027, treated with pesticides banned in the EU, could need to be thrown away if the resulting frozen chips went on sale after the deal’s implementation.
“We are very well aware of these kinds of issues and the EU is also very aware it doesn’t want to be seen to be wasting food,” Eagle said.
British exporters of produce including seed potatoes and some mussels also hope the SPS deal will allow trade halted by Brexit to restart.

“We have been waiting for this moment, but it all depends on the timing of the deal,” said Adam Taylor, a director of Taylors Bulbs in Lincolnshire, which supplies tulip, daffodil and other bulbs to garden centres and nurseries across the UK and Ireland.

A Brexit certification disagreement halted exports of British seed potatoes, particularly from Scotland, to the EU. Taylors underwent the “laborious and expensive” work of setting up an Irish business in order to keep suppling the Republic of Ireland.
“When things go back closer to how they were before Brexit, I hope our Irish customer base will reflect on the loyalty given to them,” he said.

articles.title: Swift passage of national cyber law urged
articles.summary: Amid rising cybersecurity attacks, the Cybersecurity Council of the Philippines (CSCP) yesterday pushed for the swift passage of a national cybersecurity law and urged both the government and private…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Amid rising cybersecurity attacks, the Cybersecurity Council of the Philippines (CSCP) yesterday pushed for the swift passage of a national cybersecurity law and urged both the government and private sector to review their security systems to prevent digital breaches.

In a statement issued yesterday, the CSCP, which is dedicated to advancing cybersecurity awareness and policy development, called on the government and private sector to take immediate action as cyberattacks rise faster than organizations’ ability to respond.

Citing Viettel Cyber Security’s Cyber Threat Landscape Report, the CSCP said the country recorded 16,619 phishing attacks, 255 data breach incidents and 21 ransomware attacks in the first half of the year.
These breaches exposed about 335 million records and compromised over 19.2 million Filipino account credentials.

As such, the CSCP is pushing for the immediate approval of a national cybersecurity law to strengthen the country’s defenses against cyberattacks and protect critical systems and the delivery of essential services.

“The Council urges the Senate to act swiftly on its counterpart measure so that the country has a dedicated agency, clear standards and mandatory protections for critical information infrastructure,” the CSCP said.
It also called on both the government and private sector to conduct a cybersecurity health check immediately.

“Every Filipino organization should assume it is already a target – because it is. Hackers do not wait for budgets, for legislation or for the next board meeting,” CSCP chairman Donald Patrick Lim said.

“We are asking every agency head, CEO, school president and mayor to treat this as urgent: check your systems now, close the gaps you find and train your people,” he added, noting that most attacks begin with a single click by an untrained employee.

The CSCP urged organizations to take the following steps within the next 30 days: apply pending security patches, enable multi-factor authentication on all email and administrator accounts, remove inactive or unnecessary user accounts, check employee credentials against data leaks and ensure backups are kept offline and can be restored.
To help strengthen digital defenses, the CSCP is releasing a free cybersecurity health-check guide for organizations and conducting training sessions in partnership with industry and the academe.

“Cybersecurity is no longer just an IT (information technology) issue. It is a national security, economic and public trust issue. Our country needs to move forward safely – and that requires every sector to act today, not after the next breach,” Lim said.

articles.title: President Marcos to new Navy chief: Boost territorial defense
articles.summary: President Marcos ordered yesterday newly appointed Navy chief Vice Admiral Alan Javier to boost territorial defense and deepen ties with allies.

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am
President Marcos leads the Philippine Navy change of command ceremony as outgoing chief Rear Admiral Jose Ma. Ambrosio Ezpeleta (left) shakes hands with his successor Vice Admiral Alan Javier.
Noel Pabalate
MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos ordered yesterday newly appointed Navy chief Vice Admiral Alan Javier to boost territorial defense and deepen ties with allies.
Marcos gave the directive as he led the change of command and retirement ceremony at the Philippine Navy headquarters in Manila.
Javier has been named flag-officer-in-command of the Philippine Navy, succeeding Jose Maria Ambrosio Ezpeleta.

“Build on these gains. Strengthen our ability to defend our territory and protect our sovereign rights. Deepen our partnerships with our allies and friends and sustain our commitment to the welfare of every sailor and every marine,” Marcos said.
Javier’s extensive experience in logistics, an area fundamental to the operational readiness of the Navy, will be important in fulfilling the President’s directive.

“This administration has made significant investments in acquiring new naval assets. I am confident that your experience will serve you well in ensuring that this growing fleet remains capable,” Marcos said.
The President also hailed Ezpeleta, whom he said has led the transformation of the Navy by modernizing its capabilities and advancing its role in the country’s external defense.
“Under his leadership, the Navy expanded its external defense operations, strengthened its presence in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) and intensified maritime security efforts,” he said.
Marcos said under Ezpeleta's watch, the Navy facilitated 19 bilateral and 14 multilateral maritime cooperative activities with other like-minded nations to strengthen maritime security.
The Navy also participated in 16 bilateral and 22 multilateral exercises, including Exercise Balikatan and the Multinational Exercise Cobra Gold.
“Our sailors and Marines gained valuable opportunities to work alongside their counterparts and strengthen the partnerships,” Marcos said.
Transformation

In his speech, Javier vowed to continue transforming the country’s primary maritime military unit into a “stronger, more capable and mission-ready” force amid current and evolving challenges to the country’s territorial integrity and sovereign rights.

He acknowledged “the complexities of our maritime security environment and the strategic challenges confronting our country,” considering that his previous post was commander of the Western Command based in Palawan, which has jurisdiction over most parts of the WPS.

“I understand that the demands of the Philippine Navy go beyond maintaining operational readiness. We are called upon to serve as a critical component of the armed forces to protect our people and state, to secure sovereignty and to preserve the integrity of our national territory,” he stressed.

“These responsibilities are realities that our sailors and Marines confront every day, particularly those serving on the frontlines of our maritime domain. The mandate demands not only capable forces and credible capabilities, but most importantly, the wisdom for sound judgment, sustained commitment and unity of effort that are aligned with the strategic objectives for a comprehensive, active, archipelagic defense and deterrence,” he said. — Michael Punongbayan

articles.title: Trump’s late arrival won’t delay Asean closing ceremony
articles.summary: The closing ceremony of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit on Nov. 17 will proceed as scheduled despite the late arrival of United States President Donald Trump, the…
articles.byline: Rudy Santos, Rhodina Villanueva, Mark Ernest Villeza, Pia Lee-Brago

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The closing ceremony of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit on Nov. 17 will proceed as scheduled despite the late arrival of United States President Donald Trump, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said yesterday.

“Nothing will be pushed back. We’ll proceed as planned with regard to the preparations, especially on the closing ceremony,” the DFA’s ASEAN spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial said at a media briefing at the International Media Center.
“However, the day will culminate with the ASEAN-US Special Summit. That summit will still take place despite the late arrival of the (US) president,” he added.
The ASEAN-US Special Summit will be held after the closing ceremony and handover of ASEAN chairship to Singapore.
Trump, the last world leader to arrive for the summit, is scheduled to land in Manila on Nov. 17 at 5:30 p.m., half an hour after the closing ceremony.

The ASEAN-US Special Summit is a high-level diplomatic meeting that brings together leaders from the ASEAN and the US to address shared regional and global challenges, deepen strategic ties and review cooperative frameworks.
The “only leaders” participation in the US-ASEAN Summit enable them to candidly discuss the agenda set for that summit and for identification of the measures that need to be addressed.
Imperial said President Marcos and Trump are scheduled to meet on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit and that the latter will have bilateral engagements on Nov. 18.
Trump is likely to miss the East Asia Summit, the only leader-led forum wherein all key Indo-Pacific partners meet to discuss political, security and economic challenges facing the region.
Police operations
Even as over 19,000 police officers will be deployed for the ASEAN Summit, the Philippine National Police assured the public that regular PNP operations and community patrols will continue.
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. directed regional and local commanders to maintain enough personnel in their areas to sustain crime prevention, patrols and emergency response services.
The National Capital Region Police Office, Police Regional Office 3 and 4A, as well as all Camp Crame-based units have been place under full alert from Nov. 13 to 19.
CAAP ready
The Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) said they are prepared to ensure the smooth arrival and departure of leaders and delegates for the ASEAN Summit.
CAAP director general Raul del Rosario said over 300 flights are expected to be affected by changes in schedule beginning today.
Airline companies have reached out to their passengers and promised appropriate assistance for everyone affected.
The Department of Health (DOH), for its part, has deployed nearly 300 medical personnel to respond to possible health-related incidents during the summit.
As of yesterday, the DOH has dispatched 42 medical teams consisting of 274 health care workers in venues where meetings and activities would be held.

Medical health desks were set up at the Philippine International Convention Center, the main venue of the summit, in the hotels where delegates were billeted and at the International Media Center inside the World Trade Center.

articles.title: Corruption crackdown, digitalization among new BIR chief’s top agenda
articles.summary: Newly appointed Bureau of Internal Revenue Commissioner Rolando Ligon Jr. has vowed to continue the agency’s efforts to clamp down on corruption and fast-track digitalization.

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Newly appointed Bureau of Internal Revenue Commissioner Rolando Ligon Jr. has vowed to continue the agency’s efforts to clamp down on corruption and fast-track digitalization.
Ligon succeeds Charlito Martin Mendoza Jr., who has been appointed as the new head of the Bureau of Customs (BOC).

“My commitment to the Filipino people is clear: we will transform the BIR into a fully modernized, transparent and service-oriented institution where technology empowers our tax collectors and simplifies compliance for every taxpayer, ensuring that trust in our tax system is earned and preserved,” Ligon said yesterday.
Prior to his appointment, Ligon served as Department of Finance undersecretary for the Revenue Operations Group, overseeing policies and performance tracking for both the BIR and the BOC.
Ligon said the BIR would undertake a multi-year overhaul of its core information technology systems, following recent cybersecurity incidents that may have exposed taxpayer information.

“By modernizing our computer systems, we will eliminate administrative bottlenecks, minimize room for corruption, ensure data integrity and provide taxpayers with faster, more efficient digital channels,” he said.
Ligon said the agency would continue implementing the five-point DARES framework, a reform agenda introduced by his predecessor.

This reform agenda includes Digital and Data Transformation, Audit Reform and Accountability, Revenue Collection and Base Protection, Employee Empowerment and Welfare Promotion and Service Excellence and Stakeholder Engagement.
Meanwhile, Tereso Panga is moving to the Toll Regulatory Board as its new executive director, Malacañang announced yesterday.
President Marcos also earlier appointed former Bases Conversion and Development Authority president Joshua Bingcang as the new Philippine Economic Zone Authority director general.
Bingcang was replaced by former BOC commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno.

At a press briefing, Palace press officer Claire Castro defended the recent shake-up involving the government’s revenue and investment team, saying the President wants the “right people for the right job.”
“The President is putting experience to work toward clear results, economic zones that attract investments, businesses that create jobs and government services that people can rely on,” Castro said.

Federation of Free Farmers chairman Leonardo Montemayor yesterday said Mendoza should ensure that those behind the smuggled P700-million rice from Vietnam and P524-million agricultural products found in a warehouse in Valenzuela should be held accountable.

“We want assurance from the new BOC commissioner that he will apply the full force of the law against those involved in the rice smuggling in Davao and in the Limay shipment,” Montemayor told The Star.
During inventory, the BOC recorded 99,289 sacks of red onions, 20,886 sacks of beans and legumes as well as 18,016 boxes of carrots.
The products reportedly came from Argentina, Australia, China, Egypt, India, Indonesia and Myanmar.
Sen. Francis Pangilinan said the Senate committee on agriculture, food and agrarian reform is set to investigate the attempted smuggling of around P700 million worth of rice from Vietnam.
Montemayor also questioned the transfer of Nepomuceno.
Collect Marcos estate tax by Dec. 2
Meanwhile, the 1Sambayan coalition has called on Ligon to take immediate steps to ensure collection of the Marcos family’s unpaid estate tax.
In a statement, the group said the government faces a “critical deadline” on Dec. 2, as it marks five years since the BIR issued its last written demand on the Marcos heirs.

The coalition called on Ligon to act promptly and, if legally required, issue and ensure the proper service and receipt of the necessary demand on the Marcos heirs before the applicable prescription period expires.
The estate was assessed at P23 billion in taxes in 1991, with the Supreme Court subsequently affirming the assessment. The ruling became final and executory in 1999.
With accumulated interest and penalties, the liability had grown to approximately P203 billion as of December 2021.
The group also noted Ligon serves under the President who is himself an heir and co-administrator of the Marcos estate.

“That circumstance makes the BIR’s actions all the more important – not because the Commissioner should be presumed to be conflicted, but because public confidence requires that the law be seen to operate equally,” it said.
Ombudsman sets lifestyle checks
The Office of the Ombudsman for its part said it will intensify its lifestyle checks on officials of the BIR and BOC amid reports of officials allegedly collecting bribes.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla pointed out that the two agencies are the ones entrusted with collecting money “that builds our roads, our schools and our hospitals.” — Helen Flores, Daphne Galvez, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Meralco rates rise in November
articles.summary: Over eight million customers of Manila Electric Co. (Meralco) should brace for higher electricity bills in November as rising generation costs push power rates up for the second straight month.

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am
This picture shows Meralco's electric meter.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Over eight million customers of Manila Electric Co. (Meralco) should brace for higher electricity bills in November as rising generation costs push power rates up for the second straight month.
At a media briefing yesterday, Meralco spokesman Joe Zaldarriaga announced a rate hike of P0.4895 per kilowatt-hour, bringing the overall rate for a typical household to P15.551 per kWh this month.
For residential customers consuming 200 kWh, the adjustment translates to an additional P98 on their electricity bills.
Zaldarriaga said the increase was largely due to the generation charge, which rose by P0.4344 per kWh amid the peso’s depreciation against the dollar and the ongoing global oil crisis.
Also contributing to the rate hike were higher taxes and other pass-through charges, including transmission costs, which cover the delivery of electricity from power plants to distribution networks.
The transmission charge went up by P0.1721 per kWh following the Energy Regulatory Commission’s approval of a higher maximum allowable revenue for the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines.

articles.title: COA chair named SC justice
articles.summary: President Marcos has appointed Commission on Audit (COA) chair Gamaliel Cordoba as associate justice of the Supreme Court, succeeding Amy Lazaro Javier, who will retire on Nov. 16 upon reaching the…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am
The photo of the Commission on Audit's office in Quezon City.
The STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos has appointed Commission on Audit (COA) chair Gamaliel Cordoba as associate justice of the Supreme Court, succeeding Amy Lazaro Javier, who will retire on Nov. 16 upon reaching the mandatory retirement age of 70.
Palace press officer Claire Castro announced Cordoba’s appointment as the 196th associate justice of the high court during a press conference in Pasay City yesterday.

At the COA, Cordoba led a comprehensive fraud audit of flood control projects, submitting at least 50 fraud audit reports to the Office of the Ombudsman and the Independent Commission for Infrastructure, Castro said.
He also institutionalized GPS-based geotagging of all government infrastructure projects nationwide to ensure proper verification of project status, she added.
Before heading the COA, Cordoba served as commissioner of the National Telecommunications Commission from 2009 to 2022 under four administrations, making him its longest-serving commissioner.

“He opened the industry to a third major telecommunications player, ending a decade’s old duopoly; approved Starlink’s entry in a record 30 minutes to bring satellite internet to isolated communities and cracked down on text scams and online child sexual abuse material,” Castro said.

Cordoba also served as external auditor of the International Labor Organization and the World Trade Organization, and as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Audit Institutions in 2024 and 2025.
In June this year, he received the Gawad Gat Andres Bonifacio Award, the City of Manila’s highest honor.
A lawyer and economist, Cordoba earned his Bachelor of Arts in Economics in 1992 and Juris Doctor in 1996 from Ateneo de Manila University. He passed the Bar in 1997.
Malacañang has yet to announce Cordoba’s replacement at the COA.

articles.title: President Marcos to hold bilateral meet with UN chief, world leaders
articles.summary: President Marcos will hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of Australia, Brazil, Japan and South Korea on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and related…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos will hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of Australia, Brazil, Japan and South Korea on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and related summits, according to ASEAN spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial.
Meetings with the leaders of India and Laos, as well as United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, are still being finalized, Imperial said.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, meanwhile, arrived in the country yesterday for a state visit and the ASEAN Summit, which runs from Nov. 15 to 17.

Marcos is set to meet Lula today at the Philippine International Convention Center to discuss ways to strengthen bilateral ties and expand cooperation in trade and investment, agriculture, energy, science and technology, defense and technical cooperation.

“The visit seeks to strengthen the two countries’ bilateral relations and expand cooperation in trade and investment, agriculture, energy, science and technology, defense and technical cooperation,” the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said in a statement.

“As the largest country and economy in Latin America, Brazil is a key partner of the Philippines as the Marcos administration advances efforts to broaden the country’s engagement with Latin America for mutual benefit,” the PCO said.
School protests
As the Philippines prepares for the summit, students and teachers staged protests nationwide yesterday over the government’s policies and spending priorities.
In Manila, students from several universities joined campus-wide walkouts to protest the upcoming visit of Trump.

Protests were staged at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, De La Salle University, DLSU College of Saint Benilde, University of Santo Tomas, University of the Philippines Manila, Philippine Normal University, Far Eastern University, National Teachers College and Arellano University.
Protesters at UP-Manila chanted anti-Trump slogans and performed the university’s “Unibersidad” cheer.

“His visit means that we are open arms and welcoming to imperialist leaders who do nothing but plunder our wealth and steal our future,” National Union of Students of the Philippines president Iya Trinidad told The STAR.

In Baguio City, students from the University of the Philippines Baguio, University of the Cordilleras, Saint Louis University, University of Baguio, Benguet State University, Easter College and Baguio City National Science High School marched from their respective campuses to Igorot Park for a peaceful rally opposing Pax Silica.

Meanwhile, the Alliance of Concerned Teachers Private Schools denounced the P22.9-billion allocation for the summit and city beautification projects, saying the funds could have addressed education and health care gaps instead.
The group cited the government’s P96 daily poverty threshold and said the budget could finance about 9,160 public school classrooms or more than 1,900 super health centers.

“Ordinary Filipinos will gain nothing tangible from these high-profile international gatherings while basic services across the country remain starved of support. This reflects a legacy of superficial beautification rather than genuine socio-economic development,” ACT Private Schools secretary-general Jonathan Geronimo said.
The group called on teachers, students, workers and civil society members to join a march on Nov. 15 to demand greater investment in basic services.
The Manila protesters, meanwhile, announced their participation in the protests scheduled during the ASEAN Summit from Nov. 16 to 18.

articles.title: ‘Comelec can set new BSKE date without new law’
articles.summary: Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal has disputed Commission on Elections (Comelec) Chairman George Garcia’s position that Congress must pass a new law to set the date of the barangay and…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal has disputed Commission on Elections (Comelec) Chairman George Garcia’s position that Congress must pass a new law to set the date of the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) if the Supreme Court reverses its ruling upholding the postponement of the polls to 2028.

In a statement, Macalintal said the poll body could independently schedule the elections under Sections 5 and 6 of the Omnibus Election Code, which provide for the conduct of postponed or failed elections within 30 days after the cause of postponement ceases to exist.
He argued that a reversal of the high court’s ruling would remove the legal impediment to holding the elections, allowing Comelec to set a new date without waiting for congressional action.

“Thus, if the Supreme Court reverses its decision and allows the postponed election to proceed, Comelec will have 30 days from the date of that final ruling to set the poll. This is so because on that date, the impediment or cause of postponement ceases to exist legally,” Macalintal said.
Garcia, however, maintained that the Comelec’s authority to postpone elections applies only before the scheduled election day.

“If the scheduled date for the actual conduct of the elections has not yet passed, that is why it is called a postponement. How can you postpone an activity if its scheduled date has already passed? That is the authority of Comelec,” Garcia told The STAR.
Garcia also cited the Bangsamoro region, where Congress set the date of the elections following their postponement.
Macalintal, however, argued that requiring Congress to set another election date following a Supreme Court reversal would undermine the effect of a judicial ruling invalidating the postponement.

“This grants the legislature unchecked power over election scheduling. For instance, if a postponement law is enacted just days before the scheduled polls, leaving virtually no time to question its constitutionality, the public is left without recourse. Subjecting a court-ordered election back to congressional approval would ensure that no such election ever proceeds,” he said.

The election lawyer also cited the Supreme Court’s 2025 ruling in Hagerdon v. House of Representatives, which he said recognized Comelec’s authority to conduct special elections without waiting for a House resolution.
According to Macalintal, the high court affirmed Comelec’s duty to conduct a special election within 60 days of a legislative vacancy.
He said that the same principle should apply to the BSKE, with the poll body able to schedule the elections without congressional intervention if the court reverses its earlier ruling.
The dispute stems from Republic Act 12326, which moved the BSKE from November 2026 to November 2028.

articles.title: Luistro: Defense testimony ‘self-destructive’ on VP investments
articles.summary: House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro described the defense’s testimony in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte as “self-destructive” after its witness acknowledged…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro described the defense’s testimony in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte as “self-destructive” after its witness acknowledged the official’s investment in a Jollibee branch and P2.14 million in payments she received from GenCorp Industries Inc.
Luistro was referring to the testimony of Suzette Balucanag-Punay, corporate counsel of GenCorp and Metro City Chow Foods Corp.

During the trial, Punay testified that GenCorp’s records showed total disbursements of P2.1 million to Duterte from 2022 to 2025, which she described as a return of capital from an earlier investment in a Jollibee Times Square branch.
While maintaining that Duterte was not a GenCorp stockholder, Punay distinguished the Vice President’s investment in the Jollibee branch from ownership of the corporation itself.
For Luistro, however, the testimony showed that Punay did not deny the investment.
“Even explaining that she calls it loose investment, whether loose or otherwise, it is still investment,” the lead prosecutor said.
GenCorp appears among the business interests listed in Duterte’s 2024 and 2025 statements of assets, liabilities and net worth.
Luistro also pointed to Metro City Chow Foods Corp., where corporate records show Duterte holds a 20-percent shareholding and is listed as a director.
Punay confirmed Duterte’s corporate positions, including her membership in the company’s compensation committee.
Witness withdrawals

Turning to the defense’s presentation of evidence, Luistro suggested that the withdrawal of witnesses could indicate that they did not want to be associated with or support the party that had requested their testimony.

She made the observation after noting that 18 of the 24 witnesses initially listed by Duterte’s defense team had already been withdrawn, a development she said could create a negative impression among the public.
“If there are witnesses who are declining, the easiest interpretation would be that they do not want to be identified as supporting the position of whichever party,” Luistro explained.
The withdrawals, she added, had dampened the high expectations surrounding the defense’s presentation of evidence against the allegations raised by the prosecution.

“The defense’s presentation of evidence did not begin explosively because it started with the withdrawal of a very important witness,” Luistro said. “We were anticipating explosive testimonies and/or evidence, but apparently, this was not even a firecracker. It might have been a watusi firecracker instead.”
Dollar accounts
Meanwhile, the House prosecution panel is prepared to question witnesses about Duterte’s dollar accounts if the Senate impeachment court allows it, according to Luistro.

Prosecutors were ready to cross-examine defense witnesses on the foreign currency deposits after Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) documents submitted to the impeachment court confirmed the existence of the accounts.
However, the defense opted not to present BPI senior vice president Paul Roderick Ysmael, whom prosecutors had wanted to question about the deposits.
Luistro acknowledged that the court had expressly excluded foreign currency deposits from the subpoenas because of bank confidentiality laws.
Similar restrictions also arose during the 2012 impeachment trial of former chief justice Renato Corona.
Any further testimony involving Duterte’s foreign currency accounts would ultimately depend on the impeachment court, she stressed.

“If the impeachment court allows the defense to present the witness later on regarding the foreign currency deposits, it will be up to the impeachment court. But we will definitely be very much ready to conduct our cross-examination,” said Luistro.

articles.title: SWS: Marcos administration's net satisfaction rating drops to -4 in September 2026
articles.summary: Filipino adults gave the national government a net satisfaction rating of -4 in September 2026, down from the previous survey, according to results released by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) on…

blocks.text: Filipino adults gave the national government a net satisfaction rating of -4 in September 2026, down from the previous survey, according to results released by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) on Friday.

Although SWS classified the -4 rating as “neutral,” it represented a five-point decline from the +1 recorded in June 2026, making it the second-lowest net satisfaction rating of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s administration. The latest survey was conducted from September 21 to 27, 2026.
In March 2026, the Marcos administration recorded its lowest net satisfaction rating at "poor" -13.

“Thirty-eight percent of adult Filipinos were satisfied, 18% were neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, and 42% were dissatisfied with the general performance of the current National Administration, for a net satisfaction rating of -4,” SWS said.
Performance subjects
In its Governance Report Card, SWS assessed the national administration's performance across various areas, with ratings ranging from “very good” to “bad.”

“The National Administration’s net satisfaction rating was very good on providing the youth with basic education in public elementary and high schools (+61) and improving the quality of children’s education (+50),” the survey said.

“It was good on helping the poor (+42, correctly rounded), implementing housing programs for the poor (+40), creating policies that will generate job opportunities (+40), helping victims of disasters (+36, correctly rounded), and developing science and technology (+30, correctly rounded),” it added.
The national government received “moderate” ratings for ensuring food safety, providing an efficient transportation system, and defending Philippine sovereignty in the West Philippine Sea.
Meanwhile, it received a “poor” rating for generating solutions to rising oil prices and a “bad” rating for eradicating graft and corruption in government and fighting inflation.
SWS said net satisfaction ratings declined across all 19 performance subjects compared with the previous survey.

“Compared to November 2025, when they were last surveyed, net satisfaction fell by 23 points for being prepared for strong typhoons, from moderate +28 to neutral +5, and by 14 points for helping victims of disasters, from very good +50 to good +36,” it added.
Regional ratings
The administration recorded its highest net satisfaction rating in Balance Luzon at neutral +7, followed by the Visayas at neutral -2, Mindanao at poor -17, and Metro Manila at poor -21.

"Compared to June 2026, net satisfaction with the National Administration fell by 10 points in Metro Manila, from poor -11 to poor -21. It fell by 7 points in the Visayas, from neutral +5 to neutral -2, and by 6 points in Balance Luzon, from moderate +13 to neutral +7. It stayed at poor -17 in Mindanao," SWS said.

The administration also recorded declines in net satisfaction ratings among 18- to 24-year-olds (+13 to -13), college graduates (-10 to -25), those with some senior high school through some college (+4 to -16), men (-3 to -6), and women (+6 to -1).

The net satisfaction rating improved but remained poor among those aged 35 to 44, rising by four points from -15 to -11. Meanwhile, it remained moderate among adults aged 55 and above, edging up by one point from +17 to +18.

The survey was conducted through face-to-face interviews with 1,500 adults aged 18 and above nationwide: 600 in Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila) and 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao.
The sampling error margins were ±3 percentage points for national figures, ±4 points for Balance Luzon, and ±6 points each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. —VBL, GMA News
